text: Fertilizer and nutrient management (ការគ្រប់គ្រងជី និងសារធាតុចិញ្ចឹម) should supply what the crop and soil actually need rather than applying more fertilizer to try to force higher yield. The main nutrients are nitrogen (អាសូត, N), phosphorus (ផូស្វ័រ, P), and potassium (ប៉ូតាស្យូម, K); rice, cassava, cashew, and vegetables do not share identical requirements, so a recommendation for one crop should not be transferred to another. A soil test (ការវិភាគដី) is the best basis for identifying nutrient limitations, but it may not be affordable or accessible to every smallholder -- where testing isn't possible, rely on field history, previous crops, manure/compost use, and visible crop symptoms (while noting that several nutrient deficiencies look similar and are hard to distinguish visually). During the wet season, avoid applying soluble fertilizer immediately before heavy rain, since nutrients can be lost to runoff or leaching. During the dry season, fertilizer is not a substitute for water -- a moisture-stressed crop can't use nutrients effectively, so check irrigation availability before investing heavily in fertilizer. Well-decomposed manure (ជីលាមក) and compost (ជីកំប៉ុស្តិ៍) contribute nutrients and improve soil organic matter, but their nutrient content varies, so don't treat them as nutritionally equivalent to commercial fertilizer. Splitting nitrogen applications can improve efficiency, particularly in rice, but exact timing should follow crop- and locally-validated recommendations. IMPORTANT: do not give a fixed fertilizer rate for this general chunk -- exact rates depend on crop, variety, soil, fertilizer formulation, season, and expected yield, and must be verified locally before application. If the farmer has a soil-test result or a fertilizer product label, use that to check the recommendation; otherwise direct them to a Cambodian agricultural extension officer or agronomist for an exact rate.
